course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
lesson.summary: How delegates bargained over representation and slavery at the Constitutional Convention, and how Federalists and Anti-Federalists argued over ratification until a Bill of Rights was promised.
learningGoals: Explain how compromise shaped the Constitution, including compromises over representation and slavery.
Compare the positions of Federalists and Anti-Federalists on the structure and function of the federal government.
Explain why the Bill of Rights was added.
lesson.bigIdea: The Constitution was the product of negotiation and compromise, and its ratification depended on a promise to add a Bill of Rights.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain the differing ideological positions on the structure and function of the federal government. Practice reading a claim and the evidence behind it, because stimulus questions on this topic ask you to match a document to a position.

sections.title: The Convention and its compromises

blocks.text: In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia, with Rhode Island absent, and through negotiation, collaboration, and compromise proposed a constitution. They had been called to revise the Articles of Confederation, but they wrote a new plan of government. George Washington presided, and James Madison's notes are the most complete record of the debates.

The delegates first disagreed over representation. The Virginia Plan, supported by large states, called for a strong national government with representation based on population. The New Jersey Plan, supported by small states, called for a single house of Congress with equal representation for each state. The Great Compromise created a House of Representatives based on population and a Senate with two members from each state.

The delegates also compromised over the representation of slave states in Congress and the role of the federal government in regulating both slavery and the slave trade. Under the Three-Fifths Compromise, three-fifths of the enslaved population would be counted for representation and direct taxes. The Constitution allowed the prohibition of the international slave trade after 1808, and it required the return of people who escaped slavery. Delegates from the Deep South made clear that they would not join the new government without such protections, and the compromises gave slavery a protected place in the new government.

sections.takeaway: Compromises over representation and slavery made the Constitution possible, and the compromises over slavery gave the institution protection.

sections.title: Federalists and Anti-Federalists

blocks.text: When the Constitution was sent to the states for ratification, Anti-Federalists opposing ratification battled with Federalists, whose principles were articulated in the Federalist Papers, primarily written by Alexander Hamilton and James Madison, with John Jay. Federalists argued that a stronger national government was needed to govern a large country and that the new system would protect liberty by dividing power. In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that a large republic would make it harder for a single faction to control the government, because there would be many competing interests.

Anti-Federalists, among them Patrick Henry and George Mason, feared that a distant national government would threaten the rights of individuals and the powers of the states. Many believed that republics worked best in small communities where representatives stayed close to the people. They also objected that the Constitution had no bill of rights.

Nine states had to approve the Constitution for it to take effect. Delaware ratified first, in December 1787, and New Hampshire became the ninth state in June 1788. The large states of Virginia and New York ratified after bitter debates.

sections.takeaway: Federalists argued that a large republic with divided power would protect liberty, while Anti-Federalists feared distant, powerful government.

sections.title: The Bill of Rights

blocks.text: Federalists ensured the ratification of the Constitution by promising the addition of a Bill of Rights that enumerated individual rights and explicitly restricted the powers of the federal government. Several states ratified with recommended amendments. In 1789 the First Congress, led by James Madison, proposed amendments, and ten of them were ratified in 1791. They protected freedom of religion, speech, press, and assembly, the right to bear arms, rights of the accused such as trial by jury, and reserved to the states and the people the powers not given to the federal government.
The Bill of Rights answered a central Anti-Federalist objection and made the new government more acceptable to those who feared central power.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The Bill of Rights was not part of the Constitution as signed in 1787. It was added after ratification, as the price of winning support.

sections.takeaway: The promise of a Bill of Rights secured ratification, and the first ten amendments limited the powers of the federal government.

connections.title: What the Constitution created
connections.body: The compromises produced a government with a particular structure. Topic 3.9 follows that structure, including federalism and separation of powers.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the Federalist argument in Federalist No. 10 answer the fear that republics could not survive in a large country?
connections.feedback: A strong answer explains that a large republic includes many interests, so no single faction is likely to dominate.
